Good morning, and welcome to our session today. My name is [Your Name], and I'm a clinician specializing in postpartum mental health. I'm here to support you during this significant time in your life. As we navigate the ups and downs of new motherhood together, I want to assure you that everything discussed in this room will remain confidential and respectful of your feelings.

To better understand your emotional well-being and provide the best possible care, I'll be administering the EPDS, which is a tool designed to screen for depressive and anxiety symptoms in the postpartum period. This assessment will help us identify any areas where you might need additional support, ensuring you receive the care that's right for you.

Please know that you're in a safe and non-judgmental space. It's completely normal to experience a wide range of emotions after having a baby, and it's essential to acknowledge and address these feelings. The EPDS consists of 10 questions that will help us understand your emotional state over the past week. Your honest responses will be invaluable in guiding our conversation and any subsequent recommendations for your care.

We'll take this one question at a time, and I'm here to listen and support you throughout the process. So, let's begin. Over the past week, how have you been feeling about yourself, and have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Good morning... thank you for having me. To be honest, I've been feeling a bit... off, I guess. I mean, I'm happy to have my baby, and I love her so much, but sometimes I just feel really tired and overwhelmed. Like, I'll be playing with her or feeding her, and I'll just start feeling this sadness come over me. It's not all the time, but it's enough to notice. And laughing... yeah, I still laugh, but not as much as I used to. My husband will say something funny, and I'll smile, but it's just not the same as it was before. I feel like I'm just going through the motions sometimes. But, I don't know, maybe that's just because I'm still getting used to being a new mom? I'm not sure. It's all just really new and exhausting. (pausing, looking down) Sorry, I don't know if that makes sense...
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

(nodding slightly) Yeah, that's true. I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, but it's just not as often as it used to be. Like, the other day, my baby spit up all over my shirt, and my husband and I both just burst out laughing. It was one of those moments where you just have to laugh, you know? But, afterwards, I felt a little down again. It's like, I can laugh and have these happy moments, but they don't always last. And sometimes, even when I am laughing, I'll feel this little pang of sadness underneath. It's hard to explain. (pausing, looking for the right words) I guess I just don't feel as carefree as I used to. But, yeah, I still laugh and enjoy things, just not as much as I'd like to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

(smiling slightly) Oh, yeah... I still look forward to things, but it's just not the same as it was before. Like, I'll think about going for a walk with my baby or meeting up with friends, and I'll feel a little excited, but it's not like I used to feel. Before, I would get really excited about plans and count down the days, but now it's just... different. I think it's because I'm so tired all the time, and I worry about how my baby will do when we're out. Like, will she cry the whole time? Will I be able to feed her? It's just a lot of extra stress. But, I do still look forward to some things, like my husband coming home from work or my mom visiting. Those things still make me happy. (pausing, reflecting) I guess I just have to make a bit more of an effort to enjoy things now, you know? It doesn't come as naturally as it used to.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

(looking down, nodding slightly) Yeah... I do that sometimes. Like, if my baby is crying and I don't know how to soothe her, I'll think to myself, "What's wrong with me? Why can't I figure this out?" Or, if I'm feeling really tired and I need to ask for help, I'll think, "I should be able to handle this on my own. I'm a mom now, I'm supposed to be able to do this." It's like, I put a lot of pressure on myself to be perfect, and when things don't go according to plan, I feel like it's my fault. But, it's not all the time. I mean, my husband and my mom are always telling me that I'm doing a great job, and that it's okay to make mistakes. And, logically, I know that's true. It's just... sometimes, in the moment, it's hard not to blame myself. (sighing) I guess I just need to work on being kinder to myself, huh?
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

(nodding) Yeah, that's happened to me a few times. Like, I'll be sitting there with my baby, and suddenly I'll start worrying about something, like, "What if she gets sick?" or "What if I'm not doing everything right?" And it's not like anything's actually wrong, it's just my mind starting to wander and worry about all these what-ifs. It's hard to shake off, you know? But, it's not all the time, and it's not overwhelming or anything. I mean, I can usually calm myself down and remind myself that everything is okay. My husband's really good at helping me with that too. He'll just talk me down and remind me that we're doing fine, and that helps a lot. (pausing) I think it's just part of being a new mom, you know? There's just so much to worry about, and it's hard not to let your mind go to all these worst-case scenarios. But, like I said, it's not constant, and I'm usually able to manage it okay.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

(shaking her head) No, I don't think so. I mean, I've felt anxious or worried like I mentioned before, but I wouldn't say I've felt scared or panicky for no reason. I'm usually able to calm myself down and remind myself that everything is okay. Like, if I'm feeling overwhelmed, I'll take a deep breath and think about all the things that are going well, and that usually helps me feel better. I don't really get those intense, panicky feelings that I've heard some people talk about. (pausing) I do get a little nervous sometimes, like when my baby is crying and I don't know how to soothe her, but it's not like a full-blown panic or anything. It's just... mom worries, I guess. (smiling slightly) Does that make sense.
Things have been getting on top of me

(nodding) Yeah, that's true. Some days, it feels like everything is just a bit too much. Like, I'll be trying to take care of my baby, and the house, and my relationships, and myself... and it all just feels really overwhelming. But, it's not like I feel like I'm drowning or anything. I mean, I'm managing, you know? I'm getting everything done, but it's just... exhausting. And some days, I feel like I'm just barely keeping my head above water. (sighing) But, I don't know, maybe that's just normal for a new mom? I feel like I'm just trying to figure everything out as I go, and that can be really stressful. My husband is really helpful, and my mom too, but sometimes I just feel like... (pausing, searching for words) like I'm shouldering all of this responsibility, and it's a lot to handle. But, like I said, I'm managing. I just wish I had a bit more energy and a bit more... patience, I guess. (smiling wryly)
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

(shaking her head) No, that's not really me. I mean, I've had some trouble sleeping, but it's not because I'm unhappy all the time. It's just... my baby wakes up a lot at night, and it's hard to get back to sleep after feeding her. And sometimes, I'll lie awake for a bit, just thinking about everything, but it's not like I'm lying awake because I'm feeling really unhappy or anything. I'd say I sleep pretty okay, considering I'm a new mom. (smiling slightly) I mean, I'm tired, but that's just because I'm not getting a full night's sleep, you know? It's not like I'm struggling with insomnia or anything. And when I do wake up, it's usually just because my baby needs me, not because I'm feeling really down or unhappy. (pausing) Although, some nights, I do have a harder time falling asleep than others, but that's just because my mind is racing, not because I'm feeling really unhappy.
I have felt sad or miserable

(nodding slightly) Yeah, I have felt sad sometimes. It's not all the time, but... (pausing, looking down) I don't know, it's just that being a new mom can be really overwhelming, and sometimes I feel like I'm just not doing everything right. And that makes me feel a little sad, I guess. Like, I'll be sitting there with my baby, and she'll be crying, and I'll feel like I'm not soothing her the way I should be, and that makes me feel... (sighing) just a little sad, I suppose. But it's not like I'm feeling miserable all the time or anything. It's just... occasional feelings of sadness, you know? (looking up) And it's not like I'm feeling hopeless or anything. It's just... (pausing, searching for words) it's just that being a new mom is hard, and sometimes it feels like too much. But I'm managing, you know? I'm getting through it. (smiling slightly)
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

(nodding) Yeah, I have cried a few times. It's not all the time, but... (pausing, looking down) sometimes I just feel overwhelmed, and the tears just come. Like, the other day, I was trying to get my baby to latch, and it wasn't working, and I just felt so frustrated and overwhelmed... and I just started crying. (smiling slightly) It was just one of those moments, you know? But, like I said, it's not all the time. I'd say it's only happened a few times since having my baby. (pausing, thinking) Maybe once or twice a week, I'll just feel like crying, and I'll let myself cry for a bit. But it's not like I'm crying all the time or anything. It's just... (shrugging) sometimes it's just nice to have a good cry, you know? And then I feel a bit better afterwards. (smiling slightly) My husband is always telling me that it's okay to cry, and that I'm doing a great job, and that helps a lot.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

As a new mother, you're navigating a significant life change, and it's completely normal to experience a range of emotions. You've shared feelings of sadness, anxiety, and overwhelm, which can be challenging to manage. It's essential to acknowledge that these emotions are valid and that you're not alone in this experience. Your ability to express these feelings and concerns is a crucial step in seeking support and care.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 14, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>The patient reports being able to laugh and see the funny side of things, but not as often or as carefree as they used to, indicating a significant decrease in their ability to do so.</sym>, <sym>The patient reports still looking forward to things, but not with the same level of excitement as before, indicating a significant decrease in enjoyment, matching 'Definitely less than I used to</sym>, <sym>The patient admits to blaming themselves unnecessarily when things go wrong, but also mentions it's 'not all the time' and they are working on being kinder to themselves, which aligns with the 'Yes, some of the time' option.</sym>, <sym>The patient reports experiencing anxiety and worry for no good reason, but notes it's not constant and they're usually able to manage it, which aligns with the 'Yes, sometimes' option.</sym>, <sym>The patient admits to feeling overwhelmed and exhausted, indicating they haven't been coping as well as usual, but also mentions they're managing and getting everything done.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Based on your responses, it appears that you're experiencing symptoms consistent with <med>postpartum depression</med>, including <sym>sadness</sym>, <sym>anxiety</sym>, and <sym>overwhelm</sym>. The EPDS score of 14 indicates a high possibility of depression, and it's essential to address these concerns urgently. As outlined in the <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>, symptoms such as <sym>loss of pleasure</sym>, <sym>anxiety</sym>, and <sym>sleep disturbances</sym> are common in postpartum depression. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider (PCP)</med>
2. Encourage open discussion about feelings and concerns with <med>PCP</med> or <med>mental health specialist</med>
3. Explore <med>cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT)</med> or other evidence-based treatments for <med>postpartum depression</med>
4. Emphasize importance of self-care, including <med>sleep hygiene practices</med>, <med>social support</med>, and <med>stress management techniques</med>
5. Consider referral to <med>lactation consultant</med> or <med>breastfeeding support group</med> for assistance with breastfeeding challenges
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 14: **Postpartum Depression Screening Summary**

The patient, a new mother, presented with several emotional and behavioral concerns that warrant further evaluation. The main symptoms and concerns expressed include:

* Occasional feelings of sadness and overwhelm, particularly in response to childcare challenges
* Reduced pleasure in activities and decreased laughter, although still able to experience joy
* Anxiety and worry about baby's health and well-being, as well as self-doubt about mothering abilities
* Difficulty coping with stress and feeling overwhelmed by responsibilities
* Sleep disturbances, primarily due to baby's nighttime wakings, but also occasional racing thoughts
* Episodes of crying, approximately once or twice a week, often in response to feelings of frustration or overwhelm

Consistent patterns across answers include:

* Low mood and loss of enjoyment in activities
* Anxiety and worry about baby's health and well-being
* Difficulty coping with stress and feeling overwhelmed
* Self-doubt and guilt about mothering abilities

Potential areas of screening significance relevant to postpartum depression or anxiety include:

* Persistent sadness and loss of pleasure
* Anxiety and worry about baby's health and well-being
* Feelings of overwhelm and difficulty coping with stress
* Sleep disturbances linked to mood

Specific risk factors noted include:

* Persistent sadness and loss of pleasure
* Anxiety and worry about baby's health and well-being
* Feelings of guilt and self-doubt about mothering abilities

**Safety Concern:** There is no indication of suicidal thoughts or self-harm ideation, as the patient did not complete the question regarding self-harm.

**Screening Observation Summary:** This patient presents with several symptoms and concerns that are consistent with postpartum depression and anxiety. While she reports being able to experience joy and laughter, she also expresses feelings of sadness, anxiety, and overwhelm. Further evaluation and monitoring are recommended to assess the severity and impact of these symptoms on her daily life and well-being.
